sentence: Depression is more than feeling unhappy or fed up for a few days, and it can come with physical symptoms.
note: NHS: more than simply feeling unhappy or fed up for a few days.

sentence: Treatment depends on severity and usually combines self-help, talking therapies and sometimes medicine.
note: NHS: treatment usually involves a combination of self-help, talking therapies and medicine.

sentence: People can refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service, or a GP can refer them.
note: NHS: GP can refer or you can refer yourself.

sentence: If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.
note: Crisis route, see final section.

sentence: The NHS describes depression as more than simply feeling unhappy or fed up for a few days.
note: NHS overview.

sentence: It can involve lasting feelings of unhappiness and hopelessness, and losing interest in things that used to be enjoyed.
note: NHS symptoms.

sentence: Some people also notice physical symptoms, such as feeling constantly tired, sleeping badly, or having no appetite or sex drive.
note: NHS physical symptoms list.

sentence: Because depression affects people differently, the NHS suggests a GP appointment for anyone who is concerned about how long these feelings have lasted.
note: Paraphrase of NHS 'see a GP' advice; flagged for second pass.

sentence: The NHS says a low mood that lasts for two weeks or more could be a sign of depression.
note: NHS low mood page.

sentence: Other symptoms it lists include getting no enjoyment out of life, feeling hopeless, being unable to concentrate on everyday things, and having thoughts about harming yourself or suicidal thoughts.
note: NHS.

sentence: Aches and pains can also be part of the picture.
note: Search summary: various aches and pains.

sentence: Depression can be mild or severe, and severe depression can bring a feeling that life is no longer worth living.
note: Search summary.

sentence: Life-changing events such as bereavement, losing a job or giving birth can bring depression on.
note: Search summary of NHS causes.

sentence: People with a family history of depression are more likely to experience it, and depression can also arise for no obvious reason.
note: Search summary.

sentence: Treatment usually depends on how severe the depression is.
note: NHS.

sentence: It usually involves a combination of self-help, talking therapies and medicine.
note: NHS.

sentence: For mild depression, a GP can refer someone for talking therapies, or the person can refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service.
note: NHS.

sentence: For moderate to severe depression, a combination of talking therapy and antidepressants is often recommended.
note: NHS.

sentence: People with severe depression may be referred to a mental health team of psychologists, psychiatrists, specialist nurses and occupational therapists.
note: NHS.

sentence: For mild depression, a doctor may suggest watchful waiting, which means monitoring progress to see whether it improves, alongside lifestyle measures and guided self-help.
note: Search summary: watchful waiting, exercise, guided self-help.

sentence: The NHS says even moderate exercise releases chemicals in the brain that lift mood, and that working through a CBT-based self-help guide is an option.
note: NHS low mood page.

sentence: A NICE-based summary says antidepressants should not be offered as the main treatment for less severe depression unless that is the person's preference.
note: Search summary of NICE-based advice; flagged for second pass.

sentence: Antidepressants are one option within that package, usually prescribed after a conversation with a GP.
note: Inference from the NHS page; flagged for second pass.

sentence: The NHS says symptoms start to improve some weeks after starting an antidepressant, so effects are not immediate.
note: Retrieved: symptoms start to improve within 4 weeks; number left out of prose.

sentence: The NHS advises that antidepressants are reduced gradually when they are stopped, to help avoid withdrawal symptoms, and that this should be done with the GP.
note: NHS: reduce gradually to avoid withdrawal.

sentence: The NHS says to contact a GP straight away if feelings of hopelessness or suicidal thoughts start, or get worse, after starting an antidepressant.
note: NHS: contact GP straight away if hopelessness or suicidal thoughts start or worsen.

sentence: A GP appointment is the usual first step for someone who thinks they may have depression.
note: NHS routes; flagged for second pass.

sentence: NHS talking therapies accept self-referral, so a GP is not the only way in.
note: NHS self-referral.

sentence: Many people recover with the right support. If thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life are present, help is available immediately.
note: Assignment brief: every mental-health page carries the crisis route; trust pages (gmmh urgent-help) list NHS urgent mental health support alongside 999.

sentence: If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E.
note: Trust pages: if life is at risk, someone is in immediate danger or has harmed themselves, call 999 or go to A&E.

sentence: For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf.
note: NHS trust page: call NHS 111 option 2 for urgent mental health support; 24/7; can call for yourself or someone else.

sentence: Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.
